# A Structured Complex of Means Beats More Volume or a Random Combination of the Same Means

**What it is** — The authors define training load by five characteristics: its resulting
effect (the qualitative and quantitative special work capacity produced), its composition or
contents (the complex of means applied), its structure (the correlation of means), its volume
(the quantity of training work) and its intensity (the difficulty or quality of the work).
They argue that raising training volume alone cannot compensate for a low training effect
from the means being used, but also that there is no guarantee that highly effective,
logically organized specialized means can produce the same special work capacity at a much
smaller volume in less time. Training volume is said to serve two functions: providing a
functional base for further development of special work capacity (called a universal
principle) and raising special fitness primarily through endurance development (said to be
appropriate only for certain sports). The text also states a direct correlation between
training volume and how long a training effect is maintained, and calls volume an important
condition for successful technical preparation. On structure, the authors state that "no one
means or method of special preparation should be considered universal or absolutely
effective"; each means should have its own place in a training stage depending on the sport's
specificity, the athlete's fitness level, prior training loads and the current stage's aims.
Citing Verkhoshansky (1966, 1970), Tatyan (1974) and Khodykin (1975), the authors state that
special strength training using a specific, structured system of different means and methods
produces a significantly greater effect than randomly using the same means and methods
separately, an advantage achieved even at a smaller volume of work. Figure 4.1 (verified
against the page image, PDF p. 214, printed p. 203) depicts this as three curves, "Means A,"
"Means B" and "Means C," each plotting specific training effect against performance and each
saturating at a successively higher ceiling, illustrating that different means have different
effect ceilings and are meant to be introduced in sequence as the athlete's fitness rises.
(PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 205-206.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why a structured, logically-ordered
combination outperforms a random combination at equal or lower volume; the cited studies
(Verkhoshansky 1966, 1970; Tatyan 1974; Khodykin 1975) are not described in this passage
beyond the summary claim. Inference: this is consistent with the non-commutative and
non-associative framing given in the same section
([[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): if order and combination
change outcomes, a deliberately structured combination should on average outperform a
randomly-ordered one of equal volume, simply by avoiding combinations that interfere with
each other.

**When to apply** — Inference: when training volume cannot be increased further, whether
from time, recovery capacity, or in-season constraints, prioritize reorganizing the
composition, structure and intensity of the training complex over adding more work. Use

strength work, then reactive or plyometric work) to introduce as the training effect from the
prior means saturates for that athlete.

book gives no criteria for identifying, in practice, when a given means has "saturated" for
an individual athlete, and the cited studies are Soviet-era citations not described in enough
detail here to assess their design or effect size.

failure mode this heuristic warns against. Figure 4.1's "Means A" curve, which saturates
earliest and lowest, represents that means running out of training effect, at which point a
different means ("Means B" or "Means C") is needed to keep raising the athlete's specific
training effect.

[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].

"""Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python scripts/lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STAGING = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
